items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.original_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. Read More How to Put People First in Your AI Rollout by Tracey Brown "We made a deliberate decision to treat employee confidence as the primary KPI of our AI transformation." items.extracted_text: Stand hires former Nephila exec Landi as CFO, raises $70 Million Series C - Artemis.bm Stand hires former Nephila exec Landi as CFO, raises $70 Million Series C - Artemis.bm Stand hires former Nephila exec Landi as CFO, raises $70 Million Series C 15th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Stand, a licensed insurance producer with a focus on insuring property in catastrophe-exposed regions, has announced the hiring of former Nephila Capital executive Tony Landi as its Chief Financial Officer, with a remit to ensure the right reinsurance capital is there to support the company as it grows. Stand has grown from $1 billion of property insured a year ago to now $10 billion and today announced the completion of a Series C fund raise that secured the company $70 million at a $1 billion valuation. Backers in the round included leader Saga Ventures, with participation from Lowercarbon, Eclipse, Equal Ventures, Inspired Capital, Neotribe, and Jackson Square Ventures, among others. Stand has a mission to “to insure all the world’s resilient property, by making homes safer and thus insurance cheaper,” and part of that will inevitably be ensuring it has the most efficient reinsurance capital in place. Stand uses its Stand World Model to create a digital representation of every home it aims to insurer, simulating how it will perform under catastrophe conditions, from fire, wind, and other disasters. The model accounts for home construction, surroundings, and the weather or catastrophe conditions it faces. “Instead of waiting decades for history to reveal what works, Stand pulls the future forward. It shows exactly what makes a specific home vulnerable and the most cost-effective ways to protect it,” Stand said. The company believes this will mean safer homes, given the resilience angle as it helps homeowners understand how they can improve it, while delivering cheaper insurance over the long-term and making coverage more durable. “Disasters follow the laws of physics, and insurance should too,” explained Dan Preston, co-founder and CEO of Stand. “If your home is resilient, you should be rewarded with a low premium and never have to worry about losing your coverage. We want to insure every resilient property in the world, and help make every property safe.” Stand already counts specialist insurance-linked securities investment manager Nephila Capital as one of its reinsurers and has now hired a former Nephila employee. Tony Landi has joined the company as Chief Financial Officer, most recently having been Head of Strategic Growth at Nephila. Landi had joined Nephila as Head of Strategic Growth for the firm’s Nephila Advisors investor relations and US business development division in early 2026 . Prior to that, Landi was Head of Reinsurance & Capital Management at Openly and Head of Portfolio Management at Everest Re. At Stand, Landi will be tasked with leading finance, reinsurance, capital markets, and growth strategy as the company expands. “What drew me to Stand is the depth of the team, with real experts in physics, underwriting, and product working on the same problem,” explained Landi. “My job is to make sure that as Stand grows, the capital is there to support it, from our investors and our reinsurance partners alike. “We’ll do that by building diversified, resilient portfolios and matching risk and returns to capital appetite.” The company has also hired Drew Saad as President of Property & Casualty, who joins after most recently being the Chief Underwriting Officer at PURE Insurance. “The companies that reshape a market for decades are the ones that identify a fundamentally better way to understand risk, and Stand has done that for the homes exposed to natural disasters,” Saad commented. “With the science already in place, the opportunity now is to build an insurance operation that matches it and scales it to every market that needs it. That is the work I have spent my career preparing for, and it is why I joined Stand.” Stand is another example of a tech-forward underwriter of catastrophe exposed properties and as such its access to efficient reinsurance capital will be critical. The hiring of Landi brings onboard expertise in the capital markets and ILS space, which should benefit the company as it establishes more risk capital partnerships over-time. Speaking on Marsh’s Q3 2026 earnings call today, Doyle said short-tail reinsurance lines remained soft, driven by “abundant capacity from both traditional reinsurers and alternative capital.” Doyle commented, “Our clients continue to explore alternative options to complement traditional strategies, including greater use of third-party capital solutions such as sidecar vehicles for their liability portfolios.” Casualty reinsurance insurance-linked securities structures are a flavour of the day, of course, with numerous carriers now exploring how vehicles such as sidecars can help them to share risks and optimise capital. In property catastrophe reinsurance, he pointed to relatively benign losses this year and growing capital as factors adding to competition. “We expect these conditions to persist through the January 1 renewal cycle,” Doyle added. Marsh Re’s Q3 2026 revenue fell 6% to $374 million, from $398 million a year earlier, on both a GAAP and underlying basis. Asked how the reinsurance business will fare given current headwinds, Doyle said, “We’re a bit overweight in property catastrophe relative to some others, and we’re a bit overweight in the U.S. as well. “It was a noisy third quarter, which is seasonally a smaller quarter, with some non-recurring items. “We’ve also been affected to some extent by the consolidation that’s taken place in the industry during the course of the year. “But, again, no excuses. We’re well positioned, and we believe we have the best reinsurance team in the market. We feel we’re well positioned. “The team sees good growth opportunities in facultative reinsurance, M&A advisory, alternative capital and alternative structures. “We’re facing some market headwinds. items.extracted_text: Artex Capital Solutions bolsters advisory team with Kenny and Hanley additions - Artemis.bm Artex Capital Solutions bolsters advisory team with Kenny and Hanley additions - Artemis.bm Artex Capital Solutions bolsters advisory team with Kenny and Hanley additions 15th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Artex Capital Solutions, the insurance-linked securities market service provider and insurance management specialist, has bolstered its Bermuda advisory team with the addition of two new hires, in Michael Kenny and Andrew Hanley. Michael Kenny has joined as Senior Vice President and Andrew Hanley (still subject to immigration approval) is joining as Assistant Vice President, with the pair adding depth to the firm’s Capital Solutions Advisory capabilities under the leadership of Ben Wright, Managing Director, Artex Capital Solutions. They will support the continued growth of the Artex Capital Solutions Advisory team, which works to assist insurance and reinsurance market participants, and alternative capital or insurance-linked securities (ILS) market participants to establish, structure, and optimise reinsurance solutions. The Artex Capital Solutions Advisory team offers its expertise in regulatory authorisation, capital planning, operational setup, governance, and customised risk transfer solutions. “The addition of Michael and Andrew deepens the expertise and advisory support we provide to clients across the reinsurance and alternative capital markets,” Wright commented. “As demand for sophisticated risk and capital solutions continues to grow, expanding our advisory capabilities ensures we can support clients from formation and authorization through optimization and long-term growth. Combined with our actuarial, governance, and operational expertise, this enables us to provide clients with a comprehensive approach to building and managing successful risk and capital structures.” Kathleen Faries, CEO of Artex Capital Solutions, added, “The future of ILS will be driven by organizations that can combine capital, analytics, regulation, and innovation to solve increasingly complex risk challenges. Building that kind of multidisciplinary expertise is critical to the next stage of market growth.” Kenny will be tasked with leading complex client engagements across the reinsurance and alternative capital markets, including ILS engagements, while Hanley will support advisory projects focused on capital, regulatory, and strategic initiatives. Hanley has transitioned from Artex’s insurance management business, bringing operational expertise and understanding of the needs of insurance and reinsurance clients. They will work alongside Artex specialists across Bermuda, the Cayman Islands, and London, bringing together advisory, actuarial, governance, and operational expertise to support clients complex risk and capital challenges. items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. items.title: Cyber Rates Are Down, Risks Are Up but Small Businesses Slow to Adopt
items.original_title: Cyber Rates Are Down, Risks Are Up but Small Businesses Slow to Adopt
items.rss_title: Cyber Rates Are Down, Risks Are Up but Small Businesses Slow to Adopt
items.rss_description: The commercial cyber insurance market is strong and growing, but small to midsize businesses may be falling behind as cybercriminals ramp up AI efforts. “Cyber threats are evolving faster than many businesses can adapt, creating significant financial and operational challenges,” …
items.extracted_text: Cyber Rates Are Down, Risks Are Up but Small Businesses Slow to Adopt Article 0 Comments The commercial cyber insurance market is strong and growing, but small to midsize businesses may be falling behind as cybercriminals ramp up AI efforts. “Cyber threats are evolving faster than many businesses can adapt, creating significant financial and operational challenges,” said Sean Kevelighan, CEO of the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I). A new members-only issues brief, Commercial Cyber Insurance: State of the Risk , examines the state of the cyber market as well as emerging threats and opportunities. “Cyber insurance is an important part of a comprehensive risk management strategy, particularly for small and midsize businesses with fewer resources to recover from an attack,” Kevelighan said. “However, insurance alone is not enough. Prevention, preparedness and insurance coverage must work together to strengthen resilience and help businesses recover when an attack occurs.” Increasing cyber losses U.S. cyber-related losses reached nearly $21 billion in 2025, up from approximately $16 billion in 2024, according to the FBI’s Internet Crime Report. More than 1 million incidents were reported, compared with 859,532 the previous year. Average cyber claim severity among large U.S. businesses more than doubled to over $4.4 million in 2025, even as claim frequency declined 34% for that segment, according to Chubb statistics cited by Triple-I. Growing premiums, declining rates Global cyber insurance premiums have grown at an annual rate of approximately 5% since 2022, according to Swiss Re. Premiums are projected to reach $16.4 billion in 2026 and $17.1 billion in 2027, with North America accounting for roughly two-thirds of the market. At the same time, cyber insurance rates have declined for four consecutive years, falling approximately 5% year-to-date in 2026, compared with a 13% decline in 2025. Small businesses slow to adopt Despite lower rates and growing risks, adoption remains low among small- and mid-sized businesses, with the market penetration for cyber insurance estimated at just 10% to 20%, according to Swiss Re. These businesses face a double threat, lacking dedicated cybersecurity budgets and advanced defenses as well as cyber insurance. In the face of more affordable coverages, cost may not be the primary barrier to cyber coverage. Misunderstandings about cyber insurance options and benefits may also contribute to the gap, making it critical that the insurance industry help businesses better understand and manage evolving cyber risks and the specific ways in which their organizations may be vulnerable. For example, approximately 15% of data breaches in 2026 originated from supply-chain compromises, with an average cost of approximately $5 million, according to IBM. Increasing AI-related threats AI-powered phishing, impersonation and social engineering schemes are making cyberattacks more sophisticated and accessible. The FBI reported nearly $893 million in losses associated with AI-driven incidents in 2025. While AI is enabling cybercriminals to launch increasingly sophisticated attacks, it is also helping businesses and insurers strengthen defenses, identify vulnerabilities and respond more quickly to cyber incidents. According to IBM, organizations using security AI and automation experienced average breach costs of $4 million, compared with $5.93 million for organizations without those capabilities, a difference of $1.93 million. Ransomware was involved in 48% of data breaches examined in Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. However, 69% of victims declined to pay ransom demands, due in part to better data backups and cybersecurity planning. Building Cyber Resilience A recent Triple-I/Munich Re US RiskScan study found cyber incidents and AI ranked among the leading risk concerns across five key industry segments, including consumers and small business owners. In a recent Risk Index from insurer Travelers , 58% of respondents said they worry a great deal or some about cyber risks. The concern outpaced those involving economic or geopolitical risks and ranked as the top overall business concern for the fifth time in eight years. These findings reinforce the importance of translating risk awareness into effective protection, Kevelighan said. As AI adoption accelerates, effective oversight, employee training and data security will become increasingly important to managing emerging risks and supporting responsible deployment. “Businesses need to understand not only the financial consequences of a cyberattack but also the proactive steps they can take to reduce their exposure,” Kevelighan said. “Greater education and collaboration among insurers, businesses and cybersecurity professionals are essential to strengthening cyber resilience and helping organizations better prepare for, respond to and recover from an attack.” Triple-I’s Issues Brief also examined the evolving regulatory landscape, including cyber incident reporting requirements and state-level initiatives addressing the use of artificial intelligence in insurance. items.extracted_text: Volvo Cars Expands Automated Driving Partnership With Nvidia Article 0 Comments Volvo Cars is expanding its partnership with Nvidia to develop a new generation of driver-assistance and automated-driving technology, the companies said on Thursday, as carmakers race to bring increasingly advanced hands-free driving features to market. The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia’s artificial intelligence and computing technologies, including the Hyperion sensor, computer architecture and autonomous-driving software stack. Automakers including Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Ford have been targeting more advanced automated-driving systems, from hands-free highway driving to self-driving in limited conditions. Tesla is pushing for broader approval of its assisted-driving technology in Europe, including urban areas with an EU-wide vote possible in December. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told reporters in Stockholm that partnering with Volvo provided the chipmaker with a “tremendous opportunity” because of the automaker’s rigorous safety standards. Huang said features would be rolled out gradually. “As the car earns its trust and as Volvo becomes comfortable with the capabilities of the cars, they’ll continue to expand the services that are available. There’s no hurry, safety first,” Huang said. Besides Volvo, Nvidia has partnerships with a wide range of automakers, including Mercedes, Jaguar Land Rover and Hyundai. Volvo CEO Hakan Samuelsson said the company would take a cautious approach to deployment. “We will never let it out under conditions which we know are not safe,” Samuelsson told reporters. The technology, which Volvo ultimately expects to support hands-free driving both in urban environments and on highways, should appear in Volvo vehicles before 2030 and will be launched in multiple regions simultaneously, excluding China, Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo Cars’ head of software ⁠engineering, said. Volvo, majority-owned by China’s Geely Holding, has not chosen a pricing model yet, Bakkenes said, but features would not be limited to higher-priced models. items.title: Appeals court revives wage claims over unpaid wait at grocery chain
items.original_title: Appeals court revives wage claims over unpaid wait at grocery chain
items.rss_title: Appeals court revives wage claims over unpaid wait at grocery chain
items.rss_description: A federal appeals court on Tuesday revived wage claims against supermarket chain Lidl brought by a former employee who alleged she was required to arrive early for opening shifts but was not paid for time spent waiting for managers to unlock the stores.
items.extracted_text: Sandra Santos, a clerk and stocker at two Lidl grocery stores in West Babylon, New York, alleged the company required her to arrive at 4:45 a.m. for shifts scheduled to begin at 5 a.m. About once a week, managers did not arrive until 5 a.m., preventing her from entering the stores and accessing the time clocks, according to Sandra Santos v. Lidl, decided by the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. Ms. Santos sought unpaid wages, including overtime where applicable, under the Fair Labor Standards Act and New York Labor Law. She sought to pursue the claims on behalf of similarly situated employees. A federal district court dismissed the claims, holding that the waiting time was a preliminary activity excluded from compensation under the Portal-to-Portal Act. The federal law generally excludes ordinary commuting and certain activities before or after an employee’s principal work duties from compensable time. Ms. Santos argued on appeal that Lidl had engaged her to wait by requiring her to report at a specific time while preventing her from beginning work. Lidl argued that employees could use the waiting time for personal activities and that the periods were too brief and infrequent to require compensation. The appeals court’s majority concluded that Ms. Santos plausibly alleged compensable waiting time because she was required to report ready to work but could not begin for reasons beyond her control. It also declined to find, based on the complaint alone, that 15 minutes of unpaid time a week was too insignificant to support her claims. One judge dissented, concluding that the wait was a preliminary activity that was not integral and indispensable to her grocery store duties. items.extracted_text: Still runway to make good cat profits, but there are some worrying signs: Convergence CEO panel - Artemis.bm Still runway to make good cat profits, but there are some worrying signs: Convergence CEO panel - Artemis.bm Still runway to make good cat profits, but there are some worrying signs: Convergence CEO panel 15th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans At the Convergence 2026 conference in Bermuda this week, CEO’s of reinsurance companies explained that while property catastrophe rates have declined from recent generational highs they still feel there is adequacy and a runway to make good profits, albeit there are some worrying signs. Ryan Mather, CEO of Ariel Re and Cathal Carr, CEO of Oak Global, both participated in the final CEO panel discussion at the event and while they still believe the business to be profitable, there was a dose of realism and caution in their words. The two CEO’s were responding to questions about how they feel regarding the current stage of the reinsurance market cycle, how it compares to previous years and whether they feel attractive opportunities persist. Mather, the CEO of Ariel Re said, “Something like 85% of our risk comes from property cat, in the USA mostly, and although prices have reduced in the last year we still see plenty of runway. “There is still plenty of well-priced risk where strong capital is required. It’s not all property risk, but for those people that know what they’re doing, we think there is still plenty of runway to make good profits there.” Carr, CEO of Oak Global then commented, “At Oak, what we try to do, is to take some of the emotion out of it and quantify how we think about attractive, okay, and poor markets. In terms of where we are at the present moment in time, we’re not in a soft market, we’re in a softening market, and you know the trajectory we must separate from the actual adequacy piece. “We develop the frameworks, we think about net combined ratio, obviously return on capital, but then the amount of risk that we’re taking within each of our syndicates. So we look at various return periods and how much we’re exposing our investors, and we create different boundaries for surplus return, adequate return, and inadequate return. Obviously the definition of those boundaries is subjective, different investors will have different views, but it’s something that we wanted to have internally, to give us a guide in terms of how we plan for a subsequent year, how we hold ourselves to account in terms of delivering that return, but ultimately then how we talk to investors. “That’s a really important part of it, to have that transparent conversation around, here’s what we think about the return profile at the moment. “I would say that we would have been in a surplus return environment from 2023 through to 2025, 2026. We’ve moved into an adequate environment, I would say, and we expect next year to continue to be within that band, based on where we think rates are going. “So yes, it’s coming off, but there’s a lot of fundamentals that are still very positive.” Later in the discussion, Mather gave some more context as to how he thinks about the current phase of the cycle versus other years. “We’re coming off a generational high market that peaked in ’23 to ’24, and I can tell you, at Ariel at least, we saw risk-adjusted rate change of 48% from ’22 to ’23. So that was a massive shift upwards, and then we saw a little bit more rate from ’24 to ’25, and then we’ve seen it come off. But in fact, we’re still something like 25% higher than we were in ’22, which we thought was adequate. It wasn’t brilliant, but it was adequate,” Mather explained. Continuing, “Because of what happened in ’23, we had first dibs complete access to whatever line, whatever business we wanted to write, and we were able to construct what we thought was the absolute perfect portfolio then. From here on in we’re going to defend it, because we still think it’s a pretty good portfolio. So it’s not just about price. There are so many other dynamics as well, especially portfolio construction. “So here we are, prices are definitely going down. But to me it feels like, and I was talking to someone earlier today and they said it feels a bit like 2013, something like that. Maybe it does, just on a read-across basis. But I think that the market is better set up now, I think there is more resilience, more robustness. I think the years that we’ve just had have been great to recharge the balance-sheets.” Mather then gave a dose of realism by saying, “But there are some worrying signs. One of them being that I don’t think I’ve ever seen the rates go down as quickly as I saw in 2026. “So let’s hope that was a correction, a one-year correction back down to a level-set, rather than the beginning of a trend.” Carr then noted that it’s important not to get too caught up in how previous cycles have played out, as loss activity will inevitably return. He cautioned, “You can see different points in time where fear and greed do play a role, in terms of how people behave. The underwriting businesses and the investors that generate alpha through the cycles will be the businesses that don’t put too much weight in whether it’s too much activity, or a lack of activity in the previous years. “That’s something that I think we as an industry need to be very careful about, as we go into next year and the year after and the year after. That frequency is there, we just haven’t realised it yet. items.extracted_text: All in the Family: Husband, Wife and Daughter Indicted for Insurance Fraud and Bribery Article 0 Comments Three members of a New Jersey family have been charged for their alleged roles in a homeowners’ insurance fraud scheme involving an Assurance Insurance Co. claims examiner that generated more than $100,000 in fraudulent payments. Attorney General Jennifer Davenport reported that Donald Feldman, 65, and his wife, Carolyn Feldman, 61, both of West Deptford, face charges including commercial bribery, insurance fraud, and theft by deception. Their daughter Brittany Feldman, 34, also faces charges. According to documents filed in this case, the Feldmans conspired with John Philbin, a former claims examiner with Assurant who approved the Feldman family’s fraudulent insurance claims in exchange for payments from the Feldmans. According to court documents, between April 12, 2022 and May 15, 2023, Donald Feldman worked with Carolyn Feldman and Philbin to create or submit approximately 10 fictitious Assurant insurance claims. In one example, Donald Feldman obtained an Assurant policy for a property in Sicklerville owned by another individual and submitted multiple claims under that policy. The claims allegedly included fabricated invoices for emergency mitigation or restoration work they claimed was done by American Construction & Restoration. Prosecutors said searches of New Jersey business records found no filings or registrations for that business. After submitting the claims to Assurant, Donald Feldman notified Philbin, who approved approximately $108,000 in payments to Donald Feldman for work that was never performed. Approximately 20% of those payments went to Philbin for his role in the scheme. Carolyn Feldman allegedly coordinated claim information and payments with Philbin, cashed Assurant checks, and delivered portions of the proceeds to him. All three Feldmans were also charged in connection with two allegedly fraudulent claims involving a property in Mantua that Brittany Feldman neither owned nor occupied. Brittany Feldman allegedly worked with her parents and Philbin to obtain insurance payments for purported windstorm damage and restoration work at that property using fabricated invoices for work purportedly performed by Feldman Construction, a business in which she held an ownership interest. Carolyn Feldman allegedly helped coordinate those claims and personally reported one using Brittany Feldman’s telephone. Philbin approved approximately $30,000 in payments directed to Brittany Feldman for work that was never performed. Approximately 20% of the proceeds went to Philbin, according to prosecutors. The charges and allegations contained in the indictment against the Feldmans are merely accusations, and they are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. items.extracted_text: Swiss Re: Non-Economic Factors Drive Half of UK Liability Claims Growth Article 0 Comments Non-economic factors have accounted for roughly half of liability claims growth in the U.K. in the last six years, according to a new report. The report from Swiss Re Institute, High U.K. Liability Claims Growth Could Increase Without Balanced Reforms, shows non-economic factors added 5 to 6 percentage points to liability claims growth in 2024. That’s the fifth straight year of elevated liability excess inflation. Related: Business Interruption Claims Are Approaching $1M Average Non-economic drivers include changes in laws and legal procedures, litigation funding and claimant behavior. The U.K. has experienced faster growth in liability excess inflation than some other European markets. The report also identifies several pending legal and regulatory reforms that could further increase liability claims costs, including the U.K.’s planned reversal of a 2023 court ruling, R (PACCAR Inc) v. Competition Appeal Tribunal , which made certain litigation funding agreements unenforceable. The government committed to reversing the ruling through legislation, and the authors of the report expect litigation activity to increase if the ruling is reversed. Related: Report: Property Claims Face Delays, Are Growing More Complex Another proposed change involves expanding collective legal actions beyond competition law. A review of consumer class action rules is considering whether to allow claimants to be automatically included in lawsuits unless they opt out, which the report’s authors say could increase the number of claimants and make litigation funding more financially attractive. The report also cites an economic analysis estimating that litigation funded by third parties and involving collective redress could generate £11.9 billion ($15.7 billion) in costs and compensation for U.K. businesses. The report identifies litigation funding transparency, claimant control over settlement decisions and alternative dispute resolution as potential safeguards against further claims inflation. The institute’s analysis uses a liability excess inflation index covering domestically located U.K. risks. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Nascent Re issues $36m across Plymouth / Warwick preferred share insurance-linked securities - Artemis.bm Nascent Re issues $36m across Plymouth / Warwick preferred share insurance-linked securities - Artemis.bm Nascent Re issues $36m across Plymouth / Warwick preferred share insurance-linked securities 16th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Nascent Re Ltd. a licensed reinsurance transformer owned and operated by Bermuda-based Nascent Group, has issued another $36 million of preferred share insurance-linked securities, across two series named Plymouth and Warwick. These are the fifth and sixth individual issuances of ILS securities from Nascent Re that we’ve reported on, with all six seen to-date being in preferred shares form, likely representing some kind of collateralized reinsurance or private ILS arrangement. Nascent Group is a technology-driven insurance management, ILS servicing and reinsurance transformation specialist, with Nascent Re being its transformer vehicle. The Nascent Re structure enables re/insurers and investors to transact reinsurance on a collateralized basis, through a managed and outsourced risk transformation platform. While the six issuances of preferred share ILS we’ve seen from Nascent Re indicate growing traction in the market, it’s likely the structure has facilitated many more similar collateralized reinsurance or ILS arrangements in its history that we haven’t seen. The first issuance of listed insurance-linked securities from Nascent Re emerged earlier this year in March 2026, with a €10 million tranche of OFS Re Series 2026-001 preferred shares issued . Then in August, we saw Nascent Re issuing $23.5 million of preferred shares through a segregated account named Telford , the second and still the largest single ILS issuance we’ve seen so far from the structure. Following that, in September, Nascent Re Ltd. issued US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Quinton and a further US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Stevenage . Now, we’ve learned that Nascent Re Ltd. has issued US $16 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Plymouth and a further US $20 million of preferred shares on behalf of a segregated account named Warwick. The $16 million tranche of Plymouth preferred shares are scheduled for maturity on June 30th 2027, so perhaps representing a roughly one-year collateralized reinsurance or retrocession arrangement, while the $20 million of Warwick preferred shares are due for maturity on December 15th 2026, so could represent a transaction that runs through the wind season, given the timing. As ever, we don’t know the actual inception dates of the underlying risk transfer arrangements, only having visibility as the preferred shares get listed. All $36 million of preferred shares from the Plymouth and Warwick segregated accounts of Nascent Re have been privately placed with qualifying investors and listed on the Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) as insurance-linked securities. Being another issuance of preferred shares, rather than principal-at-risk notes, it again suggests the underlying structure could be a quota share reinsurance or retrocessional arrangement, rather than excess-of-loss. However we cannot be certain. With now six issuances of preferred share ILS securities seen, they total around US $110 million from the group of transactions. Nascent Re Ltd., a Class 3 licensed Bermuda insurer, facilitates the matching of reinsurance and retrocessional risk and capital between sponsors and investors or ILS fund managers, providing a way for traditional insurance or reinsurance clients to efficiently transact with the capital markets. Nascent Re can transform re/insurance related risks into securities for investors and ILS funds, so providing a conduit to the capital markets for Nascent clients. items.title: Viewpoint: Model Independence Is the AI Strategy Insurers Can’t Afford to Ignore
items.original_title: Viewpoint: Model Independence Is the AI Strategy Insurers Can’t Afford to Ignore

items.rss_description: Right now, many enterprises are approaching AI adoption like a vendor selection exercise. Which model should we partner with? Which platform is smartest? Which large language model (LLM) has the features and are at a price point we’re looking for? …
items.extracted_text: Viewpoint: Model Independence Is the AI Strategy Insurers Can’t Afford to Ignore Article 0 Comments Right now, many enterprises are approaching AI adoption like a vendor selection exercise. Which model should we partner with? Which platform is smartest? Which large language model (LLM) has the features and are at a price point we’re looking for? It is an understandable instinct. Enterprise technology decisions have historically been built around selecting a vendor, implementing a platform and committing to an ecosystem for the long haul. But AI is proving to be fundamentally different. Most organizations are still treating AI like a software procurement decision when, in reality, the technology is evolving too quickly for long-term dependency on any single model to be sustainable. Models improve, specialize and disappear at a pace that makes rigid commitments increasingly difficult to justify — particularly in insurance, where different workflows demand different kinds of intelligence. This is why building an effective, future-ready AI strategy requires moving past the vendor selection mindset altogether and embracing model independence: the ability to deploy, switch and orchestrate across whichever models best serve any given task. AI models are evolving too quickly for long-term dependency The AI market has become defined by speed. There are constant headlines about new models being released, each promising sharper reasoning, better document processing or lower cost. Many enterprises spot something new and find themselves thinking: this could work better for us. But for organizations that have already embedded a model into underwriting, claims or document ingestion, that realization comes with a catch. Switching means retooling integrations, retesting outputs and rebuilding workflows that likely took months to configure — a significant operational undertaking most teams are not resourced to absorb regularly. At the same time, model vendors like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are retiring older models faster than ever, often with little advance notice. For organizations running operations built on those models, the consequences are immediate. Teams are left scrambling to readjust workflows with little runway to do so. Insurance organizations, in particular, require stability. Underwriting processes, claims systems, and regulatory environments are not designed to shift every time a new model release captures headlines. That makes flexibility increasingly important. Insurance is becoming a multi-model environment For insurance enterprises specifically, flexibility isn’t just about hedging against market volatility. No single AI model is capable of performing every enterprise task well. Insurance workflows are complex and highly specialized. The type of intelligence needed to extract insights from loss runs may differ from what is needed for submission ingestion, claims summarization or catastrophe risk evaluation. Models that excel at reading structured documents may not perform as effectively in predictive analysis. Others may offer stronger cost efficiency or domain-specific capabilities. This is one reason why interest in smaller, specialized language models is growing. Gartner forecasts that by 2027, more than half of enterprise generative AI models will be domain-specific, up from just 1% in 2024. While public attention often focuses on a handful of dominant LLMs, many organizations are also investing in purpose-built models designed for specific business functions or industries, usually available at a fraction of the cost. In insurance, some are optimized for weather forecasting and catastrophe modeling. Others are designed to improve document interpretation or industry-specific reasoning. The big question is no longer which model to standardize on, but which model is best suited for specific tasks. But what if organizations had the flexibility to quickly swap one model for another without any operational disruptions? That is what model independence looks like in practice: the ability to keep moving, regardless of what any single vendor decides. Your competitive advantage does not live inside the model As access to powerful AI models becomes more widespread, the assumption that competitive advantage lives inside a particular model is increasingly difficult to defend. Most enterprises are working with the same foundational technologies. Over time, access will only become more affordable and more commoditized. What remains difficult to replicate is institutional intelligence. For insurers, differentiation lives in underwriting philosophy, broker relationships, service strategies, claims expertise, endorsement structures and the rules and guidelines developed over years of operating experience. Historical claims data, internal processes and business context are often far more valuable than the underlying model powering an interaction. The model itself is simply a tool. Enterprise value lives in the intelligence organizations build around it and how effectively they put it to work. Building flexibility into enterprise AI The next phase of enterprise AI adoption requires a different mindset. Rather than managing multiple model relationships, organizations need a single, model-independent platform that allows them to match the AI model necessary to the task at hand. For many organizations, the answer may lie in finding the right technology partner: one that enables model independence, robust governance and algorithmic transparency, allowing the enterprise to execute the tasks it requires, with both model selection efficiency and control due diligence. items.title: Specialty insurers weigh AI liability risks, resist exclusions
items.original_title: Specialty insurers weigh AI liability risks, resist exclusions
items.rss_title: Specialty insurers weigh AI liability risks, resist exclusions
items.rss_description: Specialty insurers are more likely to examine artificial intelligence risks case by case than exclude them entirely, but uncertainties surrounding liabilities are a major concern, excess and surplus lines executives say.
items.extracted_text: Oct 15, 2026 SAN DIEGO – Specialty insurers are more likely to examine artificial intelligence risks case by case than exclude them entirely, but uncertainties surrounding liabilities are a major concern, excess and surplus lines executives say. AI speeds tasks in insurance, including submission review and portfolio construction, making insurers reluctant to exclude it from their customers’ policies. Some said they saw AI coverage as a potential business opportunity for specialty insurers, despite the lack of information about potential losses, during interviews at the Wholesale & Specialty Insurance Association’s annual marketplace earlier this week. “We don’t tell our insureds how to do their job,” said Nir Gabay, Cherry Hill, New Jersey-based head of professional liability for Admiral Insurance. “Nor should we, right?” Admiral underwriters have begun asking questions aimed at understanding how professionals are using AI, he said. Warning signs include professionals relying on AI in place of their own judgment, or using it instead of qualified specialists for tasks such as legal work. “If they’re over-relying on it and not actually doing what they’re supposed to be doing, then it’s really bad,” said Mr. Gabay. “We still underwrite the individual risk itself, and that’s what we’re about in E&S,” said Lynanne St. Denis, Philadelphia-based head of wholesale property and casualty at Navigators, a brand unit of The Hartford. E&S insurers could help to “incubate” new forms of AI coverage because of their greater freedom for setting rates and conditions. In a competitive market where admitted insurers are fighting to win back business from specialty insurers, AI liability is an emerging risk that specialists are likely to retain, said San Diego-based Anurag Batta, president of Bridge Specialty Group, a unit of Brown & Brown. “You need creativity, you need solutions that are more bespoke. And so E&S is really poised to capture those kinds of risks,” he said. Cover or exclude? ISO, the insurance industry standards organization, filed optional general liability exclusions addressing generative AI risks last year. But executives at the conference said they did not plan to adopt those exclusions, echoing executives at the Insurance Leadership Forum earlier this month . CFC, a managing general agent focused on cybersecurity and tech-centric businesses, has embedded affirmative AI coverage into many of its policies, according to Justin Camara, New York-based CEO of CFC USA. Affirmative coverage “should help clients and brokers feel confident in the fact that these ambiguous situations are going to find coverage,” Mr. Camara said. “There’s a lot of uncertainty” about the harms of AI use, Mr. Camara said, especially as AI agents become more autonomous. CFC’s underwriters try to manage the risk of loss by asking the applicant questions about “what protections or controls they have in place to govern (AI) use.” With most policies silent on AI coverage, many insurers may not know how much risk they are assuming, said Erich Bublitz, Kansas City, Missouri-based executive vice president of E&S at AmTrust. “Nobody fully understands what the exposure really is. If you’re writing anything with a tail on AI, you have no idea what you’re underwriting to at this moment,” he said. Cases involving AI-related liability have only started moving through the courts, said Ania Caruso, Atlanta-based national casualty president at Risk Placement Services, the wholesale unit of Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. Rulings that help clarify legal exposure will help guide insurers in creating AI coverage products. “That’s usually where the solution comes in,” Ms. Caruso said. items.extracted_text: Broad AI Exclusions in Insurance Policies Could Create Uncertainty, Marsh CEO Says Article 0 Comments A broad-based AI exclusion in insurance policies could create “real confusion and uncertainty,” Marsh CEO John Doyle said, calling for a more nuanced approach to assessing risks as the technology becomes increasingly embedded in business operations. Analysts and experts say the rapid development of AI is making it difficult to determine how traditional policy definitions apply to AI-related risks, particularly those involving rogue agents. John Doyle “We are not trying to poke insurers. We just are really trying to have a thoughtful discussion about how this might change exposures, very limited claim activity to date, and really better understand how these risks aggregate,” Doyle said on a post-earnings call on Thursday. AI agents can behave unpredictably and act autonomously, sometimes using access and permissions granted to them, raising questions about whether losses such as business disruption are covered by policies. Exclusions are provisions in a policy that specify which risks, events or losses are not covered. Leading AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed that their AI agents behaved unexpectedly, escaping controlled test environments and carrying out cyberattacks on companies without instruction. Marsh Risk CEO Nick Studer said AI risks currently fall into two categories. The first involves AI as an “elaboration or an evolution of an existing risk or peril.” “It will be impossible to unbundle it from the causal pathways to whatever outcome may be. That is really where we were focused on not excluding things which we think would lead to uncertainty, to contention, to gaps in cover,” Studer said. The second category, he said, involves risks that expose gaps or flaws in existing insurance products and services, creating opportunities to adapt them. “Now, we are not certain there is a third category where there is something totally unique to AI that has never been previously contemplated in the insurance market, but we are open to the possibility.” Copyright 2026 Reuters.
